slides.text:
A string is a read-only sequence of **bytes**. Most of what you do with it comes from that: its length counts bytes, an index gives a byte, and a cut gives a piece of bytes.

In this module you will write strings, measure and cut them, build new ones and compare them. Letters beyond ASCII come in `runes-and-utf8`, and the helpers in `strings-package`.

A normal string between quotes understands escapes: a backslash plus a letter makes a special character. A raw string between backticks understands nothing and keeps the text as it is.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
quotes   -> escapes work
backticks -> text kept as typed

exercises.title: Escape characters
exercises.guide: Special characters inside a string start with a backslash.

chunks.guide: A backslash and a letter make one special character. Type a new line and a tab.

notes.text: Ends the line, like pressing Enter.
A tab: jumps to the next column.

chunks.guide: A quote inside a string needs a backslash, or it would end the string.

notes.text: Prints a quote without ending the string.

chunks.guide: To print a backslash itself, write two.

output.text:
one
two
Name:	Ana
She said "hi"
C:\temp

exercises.title: Raw strings
exercises.guide: Backticks make a string where nothing is escaped.

chunks.guide: Between backticks a backslash is just a backslash, so a path is written as it is.

notes.text: Raw string: no escapes, what you type is what you get.

chunks.guide: A raw string can also span several lines. It keeps the line break and the spaces.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    a := "x\ty"
    b := `x\ty`
    fmt.Println(len(a), len(b))
}
exercises.explanation: In `a`, `\t` is one tab byte, so it holds 3 bytes. In the raw string `b` the backslash and the `t` stay as typed, so it holds 4.

exercises.title: The empty string
exercises.guide: A string with nothing in it is a normal value.

chunks.guide: A string declared without a value starts as the empty string, not `nil`.

notes.text: Two quotes with nothing between: the empty string.

chunks.guide: Once it has text, it is no longer empty.

exercises.title: Check for empty
exercises.guide: Print each message when the name is empty: first by its length, then by comparing it.

slides.text:
Think of a string as a row of numbered boxes, each holding one byte. The first box is 0. Asking for a box gives a number, and asking for a range of boxes gives a new string.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.

exercises.title: Bytes, not letters
exercises.guide: `len` counts bytes, not letters. Counting letters comes in `runes-and-utf8`.

chunks.guide: A plain word has one byte per letter. An accented letter takes two.

notes.text: The é is stored in 2 bytes, so the length grows.

chunks.guide: The same happens with a variable.

exercises.title: Index a string
exercises.guide: Read one position of a string.

chunks.guide: Indexing a string gives one byte, which is a number, not a letter.

notes.text: The byte at position 0: a number, not text.

chunks.guide: Turn the byte back into text with `string`.
A byte can be compared with a character literal.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `s[0]` is a byte, so it prints the number 72. `s[1]` is converted with `string`, so it prints the letter i.

exercises.title: Cut a string
exercises.guide: Take a piece out of a string with positions.

chunks.guide: A string is cut like a slice. The result is a new string.

notes.text: Bytes 0 to 3: the piece is a string.

chunks.guide: The positions count bytes from the start.
chunks.text:
month := date[5:7]
    day := date[8:]
    fmt.Println(year, month, day)

exercises.title: Split a file name
exercises.guide: Cut `report` and `pdf` out of the file name, leaving the dot out.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    file := "report.pdf"
    name := file[:___]
    ext := file[___:]
    fmt.Println(name, ext)
}

slides.text: The boxes of a string cannot be rewritten. To get a different text, you build a new string from pieces of the old one and new text. Comparing strings looks at the boxes from the left, one by one.

exercises.title: Build a new string
exercises.guide: A string cannot change in place, so build another one.

chunks.guide: `word[0] = 'b'` does not compile: a string is read only.
Join new text with a piece of the old string. The old one stays as it was.
Keep the start of the word and change the end.

exercises.title: The last byte
exercises.guide: Read the end of a string.

chunks.guide: Go has no `file[-1]`, so count from the length.

notes.text: Counting starts at 0, so the last index is one less.

chunks.guide: Show the byte and the letter.

exercises.title: First and last
exercises.guide: Read the first and the last byte of the word.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    word := "gopher"
    last := word[___(word)-1]
    first := word[___]
    fmt.Println(first, last)
}

chunks.guide: `==` needs every byte to match, so the case counts.
`<` compares from the left. Uppercase letters come before lowercase ones.

notes.text: Z is byte 90 and a is 97, so Z comes first.

chunks.guide: A string that is the start of another sorts first.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    a := "Go"
    b := "go"
    c := "Gopher"
    fmt.Println(a == b, a < b, c > a)
}
exercises.explanation: `a == b` is false because of the case. `a < b` is true because G (71) comes before g (103). `c > a` is true because `Gopher` extends `Go`.
